A pull_request_target workflow that runs a pull request's code with your secrets.

sections.h: Secrets and variables
sections.body:
Passwords, API keys and cloud credentials must never sit in your code. GitHub stores them as secrets instead. A secret is encrypted, and a workflow gets it only when it asks for it by name, as in `${{ secrets.API_KEY }}`. Settings that are not secret, such as a region or a bucket name, are configuration variables, read as `${{ vars.AWS_REGION }}`.

Both can live at three levels:

- Repository: every workflow in the repository can read them.
- Environment: only jobs that use that environment, such as `production`, can read them.
- Organization: several repositories share them, which suits teams.

Set them in Settings, or with `gh secret set` and `gh variable set`. `gh secret set API_KEY` asks for the value, so it never lands in your shell history.

GitHub hides known secret values in logs as `***`, but don't count on it. A secret that a script changes, for example encodes in base64, no longer matches and is printed in full. So never `echo` a secret, never store a whole JSON file in one secret, and if one leaks, rotate it: create a new one and revoke the old. Two kinds of runs cannot read your secrets at all: pull requests from forks, and pull requests opened by Dependabot. Both also get a read-only token, which is what keeps a stranger's code harmless.

sections.h: GITHUB_TOKEN and least privilege
sections.body:
Every job gets a token without asking: the `GITHUB_TOKEN`. GitHub creates it when the job starts, and it expires when the job ends (after 6 hours at most on GitHub-hosted runners). It only works on the current repository. Every action in the job can use it, even if you never pass it on, so whatever the token may do, every action in the job may do.

**Least privilege** means a token gets only the access its task needs. You control that with the `permissions` key:

- At the top of the workflow, set the default for every job, such as `contents: read`.
- In a job that needs more, set its own `permissions`, such as `packages: write`.
- Any permission you do not list becomes `none`, and `permissions: {}` switches everything off.

Personal repositories created since February 2023 start with a read-only token. Older repositories, and some organizations, still default to read and write. So write `permissions` in every workflow and stop guessing. Then an action in a read-only job, if it is ever compromised, cannot push a fake image or change your code.

One property surprises people. A commit or tag pushed with the `GITHUB_TOKEN` does not start new workflow runs. GitHub built it that way to prevent endless loops of workflows starting workflows. That is one reason you push the release tag yourself.

sections.h: From a git tag to an image in GHCR
sections.body:
When you push a tag such as `v1.0.0`, `release.yml` builds the image and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR), at `ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/hello-devops`. That is the package you pushed by hand on Day 16. The file in Files is the full, hardened version. Its scan, SBOM, signing and attestation steps belong to Day 52; today you follow the image-push half:

1. `actions/checkout` fetches the code at the tag.
2. The QEMU and Buildx actions prepare a builder that can produce amd64 (most servers) and arm64 (your Mac) images.
3. `docker/login-action` logs in to `ghcr.io` with the job's own `GITHUB_TOKEN`. No password is stored anywhere.
4. A `run` step writes `IMAGE=ghcr.io/...` to `$GITHUB_ENV` in lower case, because registries refuse capital letters and a GitHub user name may contain them.
5. `docker/metadata-action` turns the git tag into image tags: `v1.2.0` gives `1.2.0`, `sha-` plus the short commit, and `latest`. Its `version` output, `1.2.0`, becomes the `APP_VERSION` build argument.
6. `docker/build-push-action` builds both platforms and pushes them under one multi-platform tag (Day 12).
7. The last step writes the digest and tags to the run summary.

The image is built once, from the tag, and later stages deploy that exact image by its digest. A new GHCR package is private, even when the repository is public. To pull it, make it public in its package settings, or log in with a personal access token (classic) that has the `read:packages` scope.

sections.h: Environments: a human approval gate
sections.body:
An environment is a named deploy target, such as `staging` or `production`; Day 20 gave you a first look. The release job opts in with `environment: production`. Before that job starts, GitHub checks the environment's protection rules:

- Required reviewers: up to six people or teams. One approval lets the job go on.
- Wait timer: a delay of 1 minute up to 30 days before the job may start.
- Deployment branches and tags: for example, only tags matching `v*` may deploy.

GitHub hands over the environment's secrets only after the rules pass, so the approval also guards your credentials. A run can wait up to 30 days for its approval.

Your plan decides what you get. On the Free, Pro and Team plans, required reviewers and wait timers only work in public repositories; private repositories need GitHub Enterprise for them. And if a workflow names an environment that does not exist yet, GitHub creates it with no rules and the job runs at once. So create the environment and its rules before you push the first tag.

You work alone, so leave Prevent self-review switched off. With it on, you could never approve your own release.

sections.h: OIDC: cloud access without stored keys
sections.body:
To deploy to a cloud such as AWS, a workflow needs credentials. The simple way is to store an access key as a secret. That key lives for months, works from anywhere, and is painful to rotate. If it leaks, an attacker can use it until someone notices.

OpenID Connect (OIDC) gets rid of the stored key. It works in five steps:

1. The job asks GitHub for a signed ID token. This needs `id-token: write` in `permissions`, which grants nothing else.
2. The token states facts: this repository, this branch or environment, this workflow.
3. The job sends the token to AWS and asks to use an IAM role.
4. AWS checks GitHub's signature and compares the facts with the role's trust policy.
5. If they match, AWS returns keys that expire after one hour by default.

You don't code any of this yourself. The `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` action handles steps 1, 3 and 5; you give it the role's ARN and a region. The worked example shows the workflow side, and Day 29 creates the IAM role and its trust policy for real.

`release.yml` asks for `id-token: write` too, for a different reason. cosign uses the same kind of token to sign the image without any stored key (Day 52).

sections.h: Pin actions, and let Dependabot move the pins
sections.body:
Every action you call is someone else's code, running with your token and your secrets. A tag such as `v4` is only a label, and whoever controls the action's repository can move it to different code. In March 2025 that really happened: the tags of the popular `tj-actions/changed-files` action were moved to a malicious commit that printed CI secrets into workflow logs ([CISA alert](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-github-action-cve-2025-30066)). In March 2026 it happened again, to the tags of `aquasecurity/trivy-action`, which `release.yml` itself uses; Day 52 tells that story.

A full commit SHA cannot be moved. So pin third-party actions to one, and keep the version in a comment, as in `uses: docker/login-action@81c6f93d4bc991e510b342a00b419b3bb4efc5c6 # v4.7.0`. `git ls-remote --tags` on the action's repository lists every tag with its SHA. The lab pins every third-party action in `release.yml` and `ci.yml`, and keeps GitHub's own `actions/...` on major tags. Stricter teams pin those too. Pin in CI as well as in the release: both use the same Docker layer cache, so a bad action in CI could slip something into a release.

Pins go stale, so let Dependabot move them. The lab's `dependabot.yml` does three things:

- It checks every action weekly, including the Day 20 composite action, whose folder it must be told about.
- It suggests a new release only once that release is 7 days old.
- It groups all updates into one pull request, which your CI tests like any other.

GitHub also has a newer option, in public preview: a lockfile, `.github/workflows/actions.lock`, written by the `gh actions-lock` extension. It pins every action, including the actions your actions use. It may still change, so this course sticks with SHA pins.

sections.h: Pull requests from forks: pull_request or pull_request_target
sections.body:
Most attacks on pipelines follow one pattern: untrusted code or text reaches a job that holds secrets. The trigger you choose decides a lot.

`pull_request` is the safe default. For a PR from a fork it runs the PR's own code, but with a read-only token and no secrets. A stranger's code can run, and it finds nothing worth stealing.

`pull_request_target` runs in the context of your default branch instead: your workflow file, your secrets, and a token that can write. That is safe as long as the job never runs code from the pull request. The classic mistake is to check out the PR's head commit and then run its build script or tests. Now the stranger's code runs with your secrets. GitHub's Security Lab calls this a pwn request.

GitHub is closing this hole step by step:

- `actions/checkout@v7` refuses to check out fork PR code under `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run`, unless you set `allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true`.
- A default policy will block `pull_request_target` in public repositories that have no event policy of their own. It runs in evaluate mode now, and GitHub's docs give 2 December 2026 as the date enforcement starts.
- Runs from untrusted triggers like this one can read the default branch's cache but not write to it (Day 19).

My rule: use `pull_request` for CI. Reach for `pull_request_target` only for jobs that never touch PR code, such as adding a label.

name: deploy
on: push
permissions: write-all

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - run: echo "Using key ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}"

steps.say: Ask actionlint first. It finds one problem: the commit message is text anyone with push access controls, pasted straight into a script (Day 20). It says nothing about the other four, because they are valid YAML. Tools catch some problems; you catch the rest.

.github/workflows/deploy.yml:9:34: "github.event.head_commit.message" is potentially untrusted. avoid using it directly in inline scripts. instead, pass it through an environment variable. see https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use#good-practices-for-mitigating-script-injection-attacks for more details [expression]
  |
9 |       - run: echo "Deploying ${{ github.event.head_commit.message }}"

steps.say: The other four: it deploys from any branch, its token can write everything, it prints a secret, and it uses long-lived AWS keys. Fix the trigger and the default permissions first, and pass the commit message through `env`.
steps.code:

on:

    branches: [main]
permissions:

steps.code:
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write

Finish the switch. The IAM role's trust policy accepts only tokens from this repository's production environment (Day 29 builds one). Store the role and bucket as variables, delete the old key secrets here, and deactivate the keys in AWS so a leaked copy is useless.

code.title: .github/workflows/release.yml
code.src:
name: release

# Runs when you push a version tag such as v1.2.0.
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]

# Default for every job: the GITHUB_TOKEN can only read the repository.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  image:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    # Approval gate: add required reviewers to "production" in
    # Settings > Environments. Without rules, the job just runs.
    environment: production
    # This job alone gets more rights, and only the ones it needs.
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write # push images to GHCR
      id-token: write # ask GitHub for an OIDC token, used for keyless signing (Day 52)
      attestations: write # store provenance and SBOM attestations (Day 52)
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # Third-party actions are pinned to a full commit SHA.
      # The comment shows the version. Dependabot keeps both up to date.
      - name: Set up QEMU (to build arm64 on an amd64 runner)
        uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@99012661954931238ded8c8b007157a8430204e1 # v4.4.0
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@f87e5991a6d7451dcb8d9637bfbc97413f497069 # v4.4.1

      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@81c6f93d4bc991e510b342a00b419b3bb4efc5c6 # v4.7.0
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Registries need lower case names, and a GitHub user name may have capitals.
      - name: Set the image name
        run: echo "IMAGE=ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      - name: Work out image tags and labels
        id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@dc802804100637a589fabce1cb79ff13a1411302 # v6.2.0
        with:
          images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}
          # Tag v1.2.0 gives 1.2.0, sha-<short commit> and latest.
          tags: |
            type=semver,pattern={{version}}
            type=sha

      # Day 52, step 1: build for this runner only and load the image into
      # the local Docker engine. Nothing is pushed yet.
      - name: Build the image for scanning
        uses: docker/build-push-action@c3c9e263c25d99ce0380d002d59b67737d91b0dc # v7.4.0
        with:
          context: .
          load: true
          tags: hello-devops:scan
          build-args: APP_VERSION=${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          cache-from: type=gha

      # Day 52, step 2: stop the release on HIGH or CRITICAL issues that have a fix.
      - name: Scan the image with Trivy
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 # v0.36.0
        with:
          image-ref: hello-devops:scan
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          ignore-unfixed: true
          exit-code: "1"

      - name: Build and push (amd64 and arm64)
        id: build
        uses: docker/build-push-action@c3c9e263c25d99ce0380d002d59b67737d91b0dc # v7.4.0
        with:
          context: .
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          # The app reports this version at "/" (1.2.0 for tag v1.2.0).
          build-args: APP_VERSION=${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

      # Day 52, step 3: write the ingredient list (SBOM) of the pushed image.
      - name: Create an SBOM (SPDX format)
        uses: anchore/sbom-action@66cbf4bc1f1c0d2edc94016e65bc221b6bb0ad6c # v0.24.3
        with:
          image: ${{ env.IMAGE }}@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          format: spdx-json
          output-file: sbom.spdx.json

      # Day 52, step 4: sign the image by its digest. Keyless: no private key to
      # store or leak. The signature is tied to this workflow's identity.
      - name: Install cosign
        uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@6f9f17788090df1f26f669e9d70d6ae9567deba6 # v4.1.2
      - name: Sign the image
        env:
          DIGEST: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
        run: cosign sign --yes "${IMAGE}@${DIGEST}"

      # Day 52, step 5: record how the image was built (SLSA provenance) and
      # attach the SBOM. Free for public repositories. Storage records only
      # work for repositories owned by an organization, so they are off here.
      - name: Attest build provenance
        uses: actions/attest@v4
        with:
          subject-name: ${{ env.IMAGE }}
          subject-digest: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          push-to-registry: true
          create-storage-record: false
      - name: Attest the SBOM
        uses: actions/attest@v4
        with:
          subject-name: ${{ env.IMAGE }}
          subject-digest: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          sbom-path: sbom.spdx.json
          push-to-registry: true
          create-storage-record: false

      - name: Show the image digest in the run summary
        env:
          DIGEST: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          TAGS: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
        run: |
          {
            echo "### Pushed and signed image"
            echo "Digest: \`$DIGEST\`"
            echo '```'
            echo "$TAGS"
            echo '```'
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

code.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml (final: third-party actions pinned)
code.src:
name: ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    # Skip CI on main when a push only changes Markdown files.
    # Never filter pull_request like this: a required check that never runs
    # stays "Pending" and blocks the merge.
    paths-ignore:
      - "**.md"
  pull_request:
  # The Run workflow button. Its input can switch the smoke test off.
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      smoke-test:
        description: "Start the CI image and call it after the build"
        type: boolean
        default: true

# One run per branch or pull request. A new push cancels the older run,
# except on main, where every merge gets a full result.
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}

# The GITHUB_TOKEN in this workflow can only read the repository.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      # Our own composite action: Python, the pip cache and dependencies.
      # It lives in this repository, so it only works after checkout.
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-app
      - name: Lint and format check
        run: ruff check . && ruff format --check .

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    strategy:
      # Let every Python version finish, so you see all failures at once.
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.13", "3.14"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-app
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
      - name: Run tests
        run: pytest -q --junitxml=reports/junit.xml
      - name: Upload test report
        # Upload even when tests fail: that is when you need the report most.
        if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: junit-py${{ matrix.python-version }}
          path: reports/junit.xml
          retention-days: 7

  build:
    # Start only when lint and every test job have passed.
    needs: [lint, test]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      # Third-party actions are pinned to a full commit SHA (Day 21), the same
      # pins as release.yml. Dependabot keeps them up to date.
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@f87e5991a6d7451dcb8d9637bfbc97413f497069 # v4.4.1

      # A step output: a version for this CI image, such as 0.0.0-ci.1a2b3c4.
      - name: Work out a version for this build
        id: meta
        run: echo "version=0.0.0-ci.${GITHUB_SHA::7}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Build the image (no push)
        uses: docker/build-push-action@c3c9e263c25d99ce0380d002d59b67737d91b0dc # v7.4.0
        with:
          context: .
          push: false
          # Also load the image into the runner's Docker, so a step can run it.
          load: true
          tags: hello-devops:ci
          build-args: APP_VERSION=${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          # Reuse image layers from earlier runs (GitHub Actions cache).
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

      # An image that builds can still crash at start. Run it and call it.
      # Skipped only on a manual run with the smoke-test box unticked.
      - name: Smoke test the image
        id: smoke
        if: ${{ github.event_name != 'workflow_dispatch' || inputs.smoke-test }}
        env:
          VERSION: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
        run: |
          docker run -d --name smoke -p 8000:8000 hello-devops:ci
          # Gunicorn needs a moment to start, so retry for up to 10 seconds.
          curl -fsS --retry 10 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 1 localhost:8000/healthz
          GOT=$(curl -fsS localhost:8000/ | jq -r .version)
          echo "The app reports version $GOT"
          test "$GOT" = "$VERSION"

      - name: Show the app's logs if the smoke test failed
        if: ${{ failure() && steps.smoke.outcome == 'failure' }}
        run: docker logs smoke

      - name: Write the run summary
        if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        env:
          VERSION: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          SMOKE: ${{ steps.smoke.outcome }}
        run: |
          {
            echo "### CI image"
            echo "- Version: \`$VERSION\`"
            echo "- Smoke test: $SMOKE"
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

code.src:
# Dependabot opens pull requests when the actions you use have a newer
# version. It also updates SHA pins and the version comments next to them.
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "github-actions"
    # "/" covers .github/workflows. A composite action in its own folder
    # (Day 20) must be listed too, or Dependabot never looks inside it.
    directories:
      - "/"
      - "/.github/actions/*"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
    # Suggest a new release only after it is 7 days old, so a broken or
    # bad release has time to be noticed before it reaches you.
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7
    # One pull request for all action updates, instead of one per action.
    groups:
      actions:
        patterns: ["*"]

explain_back.prompt: Explain how your release workflow keeps credentials safe, in 3 to 4 sentences. Mention GITHUB_TOKEN permissions, the environment and SHA pinning.
explain_back.answer: The workflow gives every job a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN, and only the image job gets packages: write, so nothing else can push. That token is created for the job and expires when the job ends, so there is no long-lived password to leak. The job uses the production environment, so it waits for my approval before it runs and before any environment secrets are released. The third-party actions are pinned to full commit SHAs, so nobody can swap their code by moving a tag, and Dependabot proposes updates that go through CI.

recap: Secrets are encrypted and read by name. Never print them, and rotate any that leak; fork and Dependabot PRs get none.
Set permissions: contents: read at the top, and grant more only in the job that needs it.
A v* tag triggers release.yml, which builds amd64 and arm64 images once and pushes them to GHCR.
Environments with required reviewers pause a job until a person approves it.
OIDC replaces long-lived cloud keys with short-lived ones tied to your repository and environment.
Pin third-party actions to full SHAs, let Dependabot move the pins, and keep PR code away from pull_request_target.

check.q: A job only runs tests and then posts a comment on the PR. Which permissions fit least privilege?
options: permissions: write-all
contents: read and pull-requests: write
contents: write and packages: write
No permissions key at all
check.why: The job needs to read code and write one comment. It needs nothing else.

check.q: A new teammate wants to deploy to AWS by saving an IAM user's access key as a repository secret. What do you suggest?
options: Use OIDC with an IAM role and short-lived keys
Put the key in the workflow file so it gets reviewed
Base64 encode the key before saving it
Save the key as a variable so it is easy to see
check.why: With OIDC each job gets keys that expire soon, and there is no stored secret left.

check.q: Outside contributors send PRs to your public repo, and the tests need a private registry password. A teammate suggests pull_request_target with a checkout of the PR head. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing, because pull_request_target never runs on forks
The tests would run on main instead of the PR
It costs more runner minutes than pull_request
The PR's own code would run with your secrets and a write token
check.why: That is the pwn request pattern. pull_request_target gives the job your secrets, and checking out the PR head runs a stranger's code with them.

interview.q: Why use OIDC instead of storing cloud access keys in CI?
interview.a: Stored keys live a long time and work from anywhere. If one leaks, an attacker has access until someone notices and rotates it. With OIDC, the workflow proves who it is with a signed token, and the cloud returns credentials that expire soon. The cloud's trust policy can limit access to one repository, branch or environment. There is no stored secret to leak or rotate, and each role can follow least privilege.

interview.q: How do you protect a CI/CD pipeline from a compromised third-party action?
interview.a: I pin every third-party action to a full commit SHA, so a moved tag cannot change the code I run. I review Dependabot's update PRs, which wait a few days after each release. I keep the GITHUB_TOKEN read-only by default and grant write access only to the job that needs it. I keep deploy credentials in environments behind approvals, and prefer OIDC over stored keys. I also use fewer actions where a short shell step will do.

interview.q: What is the difference between pull_request and pull_request_target?
interview.a: pull_request runs the pull request's own code. For forks it gets a read-only token and no secrets, so it is safe for CI. The pull_request_target trigger runs the workflow from the default branch with the repository's secrets and a write token. That is useful for labelling or commenting on fork PRs. It becomes dangerous when the job checks out and runs the PR's code, because then a stranger's code runs with those secrets. GitHub's checkout v7 refuses that by default, and a default policy will block the trigger in public repositories.

deeper.body:
The ID token that GitHub gives your job is a JSON Web Token (JWT): a small JSON document, signed by GitHub and encoded as text. Its fields are called claims. Four of them matter most:

- `iss` (issuer) is `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`, so the cloud knows who signed it.
- `aud` (audience) says who the token is for; the AWS action asks for `sts.amazonaws.com`.
- `sub` (subject) says which workflow is calling, for example `repo:octo-org/octo-repo:environment:production`.
- `exp` says when the token expires.

The checking happens on the cloud side. The IAM role's trust policy decides which tokens it accepts. A strict policy checks `aud` and the exact `sub`. A loose policy, such as one that matches `repo:octo-org/*`, lets every repository owned by `octo-org` assume the role. Always pin `sub` to one repository, plus a branch or an environment.

The `sub` value depends on the job:

- A job with `environment: production` gets a subject ending in `environment:production`.
- A job running on a branch gets one ending in `ref:refs/heads/main`.
- A job started by a pull request gets one ending in `pull_request`.

So you can give the production role only to production jobs, and a read-only role to pull request jobs.

One recent change affects your repository. Repositories created after July 15, 2026 use an immutable subject format that includes numeric IDs, for example `repo:octo-org@123456/octo-repo@456789:ref:refs/heads/main`. This stops someone who later takes over a deleted account name from matching an old trust policy. Your hello-devops repository is new, so copy the exact format from the [OIDC reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/oidc) when you write the trust policy on Day 29.

Ask for `id-token: write` only in the job that needs it, not for the whole workflow. And pair OIDC with environments. Protection rules must pass before the job reaches a runner, so no token exists until a person has approved.

recap: Change code on small, short-lived branches, and merge through pull requests that a reviewer and CI both check.
CI tests every change. With continuous delivery a person picks the release moment; with continuous deployment nobody does.
A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows: an event starts it, and each job runs its steps on a fresh runner.
The lab's ci.yml lints, tests on Python 3.13 and 3.14, keeps a JUnit report, builds the image and smoke-tests it.
Caches make repeat runs fast but can vanish; artifacts are a run's outputs and need unique names.
A ruleset on main with every required check stops red pull requests from merging.
Expressions are filled in before the shell runs; every if gets a hidden success() unless you write a status function.
Step outputs, job outputs and needs carry values between steps and jobs; composite actions and reusable workflows remove repetition.
release.yml turns a v* tag into one amd64 and arm64 image in GHCR, behind an approval, with a least-privilege token.
Pin third-party actions to commit SHAs, let Dependabot move the pins, and keep PR code away from pull_request_target.

flashcards.front: Continuous delivery vs continuous deployment?
flashcards.back: Delivery: every change is ready to release, and a person clicks release. Deployment: every passing change goes live on its own.

flashcards.front: What does 'build once, deploy many' mean?
flashcards.back: Build the image one time, then promote that same digest through every environment.

flashcards.front: Merge vs rebase?
flashcards.back: A merge joins two lines of work with a merge commit. A rebase replays your commits on top of the other branch, with new IDs.

flashcards.front: In semver 2.4.1, which number changes for a compatible bug fix?
flashcards.back: PATCH, so the next version is 2.4.2.

flashcards.front: Where must workflow files live?
flashcards.back: In .github/workflows/ at the repository root, as .yml or .yaml files.

flashcards.front: Which runner label gives you arm64 Linux, like an Apple Silicon Mac?
flashcards.back: ubuntu-24.04-arm (ubuntu-latest is x64).

flashcards.front: What do standard GitHub-hosted runners cost in a public repository?
flashcards.back: Nothing. Private repositories draw from a monthly allowance, $12 on the Free plan.

flashcards.front: What does needs: [lint, test] do on a job?
flashcards.back: The job waits for lint and test to succeed. If either fails, this job is skipped.

flashcards.front: Why not require only the last job of a needs chain?
flashcards.back: If an earlier job fails, the last job is skipped, and GitHub counts a skipped check as passed.

flashcards.front: Why put paths-ignore on push but not on pull_request?
flashcards.back: A required check skipped by a path filter stays Pending and blocks the merge.

flashcards.front: What goes into the setup-python pip cache key?
flashcards.back: The OS and CPU, the Python version, and a hash of the requirements files.

flashcards.front: Cache vs artifact?
flashcards.back: A cache speeds up future runs and can be evicted. An artifact is an output of one run that people download.

flashcards.front: When does GitHub work out ${{ }} expressions?
flashcards.back: Before the step runs, on GitHub's side, by pasting the value into the text.

flashcards.front: What hidden condition does every if get?
flashcards.back: success(), unless the if already uses a status function such as failure() or always().

flashcards.front: How does a value get from job A to job B?
flashcards.back: Step output via $GITHUB_OUTPUT, mapped in A's outputs, read in B as needs.A.outputs.name.

flashcards.front: Composite action vs reusable workflow?
flashcards.back: A composite action is several steps used as one step. A reusable workflow is whole jobs called with on: workflow_call.

flashcards.front: What does permissions: contents: read at the top of a workflow do?
flashcards.back: It makes the GITHUB_TOKEN read-only for code in every job, and sets every permission you don't list to none.

flashcards.front: Which permission lets a job request an OIDC token?
flashcards.back: id-token: write. It grants no other access.

flashcards.front: Why pin an action to a full commit SHA?
flashcards.back: Whoever controls the action's repository can move a tag to other code. A full commit SHA always means the same code.

flashcards.front: What is a pwn request?
flashcards.back: A pull_request_target workflow that checks out and runs a pull request's code, so a stranger's code gets your secrets.

quiz.q: A colleague's branch has lived for three weeks and touches 40 files. What problem is most likely at merge time?
options: Big merge conflicts and a review nobody can check well
GitHub refuses branches older than two weeks
The tags on main move to the branch
CI stops running on old branches
quiz.why: Branches that live long and grow big drift away from main. Conflicts pile up, and reviewers can only skim.

quiz.q: Which event lets you start a workflow with a button in the Actions tab?
options: schedule
repository_dispatch
workflow_dispatch
pull_request
quiz.why: workflow_dispatch adds the Run workflow button, once the workflow file is on the default branch.

quiz.q: Why does the lab's ci.yml put the Python version in the artifact name?
options: GitHub sorts artifacts by Python version
upload-artifact only accepts names with numbers
It makes the pip cache key match
Each matrix job needs a unique artifact name
quiz.why: Each matrix job uploads its own report, and two artifacts in one run cannot have the same name.

quiz.q: A PR run on branch `fix-typo` looks for a pip cache. Where can the cache it restores come from?
options: Any branch in the repository, newest first
Its own pull request or the default branch
Only caches made on your laptop
Other open pull requests on the same base
quiz.why: Runs restore caches from their own scope and from the default (or base) branch. A cache saved by one pull request is not shared with others.

quiz.q: In the lab's build job, the step `Show the app's logs` has `if: ${{ failure() && steps.smoke.outcome == 'failure' }}`. The image build fails. Does the logs step run?
options: Yes, because failure() is true
Yes, because logs steps always run
No, because the smoke test was skipped, not failed
No, because failure() only works at job level
quiz.why: failure() is true, but the smoke step never ran, so its outcome is skipped and the second half is false.

quiz.q: You want three test jobs in hello-devops to share the same five setup steps. Which tool fits best?
options: A composite action in .github/actions
A reusable workflow per test job
A schedule trigger
A new repository for the steps
quiz.why: Shared steps inside a job are what composite actions are for. A reusable workflow replaces whole jobs.

quiz.q: In release.yml, which permission lets the GITHUB_TOKEN push images to GHCR?
options: contents: write
packages: write
id-token: write
actions: write
quiz.why: GHCR is part of GitHub Packages, so the token needs packages: write to push there.

quiz.q: Every production release must wait for a human. The repository is public, on the Free plan. What do you use?
options: A wait timer of 60 minutes
A repository secret named APPROVAL
A schedule trigger
An environment with required reviewers
quiz.why: Required reviewers on an environment pause the job until one of them approves.

quiz.q: A CI step ends with `grep ERROR app.log`, and the log contains no errors. What happens to the step?
options: It passes, because no errors were found
It fails, because grep exits with 1 when nothing matches
It passes with a warning about the empty result
It fails, because grep needs sudo
quiz.why: grep exits with 1 when it finds no match, and any non-zero exit code fails the step.

quiz.q: You start hello-devops with `python app.py` and run `curl localhost:8000` in the same second. curl says 'Connection refused'; two seconds later it works. What did the first error tell you?
options: A firewall on your Mac blocked port 8000 for a moment
DNS could not resolve the name localhost yet
Nothing listened on port 8000 yet; the app was starting
The request timed out because the network was slow
quiz.why: Connection refused means the machine answered but no process listened on the port yet. That is why the lab's smoke test retries for a few seconds.
